sections.content: This lesson doesn't teach new grammar: it combines the tools you've already met — *aki/akik* for people (in any case: *aki*, *akit*, *akinek*), *amely/amelyek* for things, and *ahol/amikor* for places and times — into longer, natural sentences. This is exactly the shape of a good naturalization-interview answer to a question like: "Tell me about the Árpád dynasty."

items.spanish: Az Árpád-ház, amely Árpád fejedelemtől származott, közel négyszáz évig adta Magyarország királyait.
items.english: The Árpád dynasty, which descended from Prince Árpád, provided Hungary's kings for nearly four hundred years.

items.spanish: III. András, akit 'a velenceinek' is neveztek, és aki 1301-ben halt meg örökös nélkül, volt az utolsó Árpád-házi király.
items.english: Andrew III, who was also called 'the Venetian' and who died in 1301 without an heir, was the last Árpád-house king.

items.spanish: Miután a fiúág kihalt, olyan hatalmi harc kezdődött, amelyben több főúr és külföldi jelölt is versengett a koronáért.
items.english: After the male line died out, a power struggle began in which several magnates and foreign candidates competed for the crown.

sections.content: A strong summary sentence usually stacks two or three of these clauses: who someone was (*aki*), what happened to or because of them (*akit/akinek*), and what thing, place or moment is tied to that (*amely/ahol/amikor*). Practice building sentences this way — it's exactly the kind of answer that shows real command of the material, not just a list of memorized dates.
